pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Coral Bleaching & Acidification (ages 12–13): two distinct human-driven threats to reefs, one thermal (bleaching) and one chemical (acidification), both traced from atmospheric CO2 and rising temperature to reef collapse.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS3 biology — relationships in an ecosystem, and the interdependence of organisms; KS3 chemistry — the carbon cycle and combustion of fossil fuels adding CO2; builds on KS2 Y6 adaptation/interdependence.
• Standards — US (NGSS): MS-LS2-4 (construct an argument that changes to physical/biological components of an ecosystem affect populations); MS-ESS3-3/MS-ESS3-5 (human impacts and factors causing rise in global temperatures); MS-LS2-1 (resource availability limits populations).
• Operational details — Separate the two mechanisms explicitly so they are not conflated. BLEACHING: coral is an animal in mutualism with zooxanthellae (photosynthetic algae in its tissue that give it colour and most of its food); heat stress makes coral expel the algae, turning it white and starving it — reversible if brief, fatal if prolonged. ACIDIFICATION: ~25–30% of emitted CO2 dissolves into seawater, forming carbonic acid, lowering pH and reducing carbonate ions coral needs to build its calcium-carbonate skeleton — so growth slows and skeletons can dissolve. Reefs host ~25% of marine species, so reef loss is a habitat-loss cascade. End on evaluating responses (emissions cuts vs local restoration/heat-tolerant coral).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete, ~11–12): can state that too-warm water makes coral turn white and that this harms it. Tier B (transitional, ~12–13): explains bleaching as coral expelling its algae partner and links extra CO2 to more acidic water that weakens skeletons. Tier C (formal, ~13): distinguishes the thermal mechanism from the chemical (carbonic acid, ↓pH, ↓carbonate) and reasons about why reef loss propagates to ~25% of marine species and which interventions target which cause.
bestPractices: Teach the two threats as SEPARATE mechanisms with a shared root cause (emissions) — do not let students merge 'hot' and 'acidic' into one vague 'pollution' story; contrast them side by side.
Anchor bleaching in the mutualism first: students must know the coral animal depends on the algae for colour AND food before 'expelling the algae' means anything.

Make the reversible-vs-fatal threshold explicit — brief stress recovers, prolonged stress kills — so students grasp why the DURATION and frequency of marine heatwaves matter, not just peak temperature.

Connect the chemistry to the biology causally: CO2 → carbonic acid → ↓pH → fewer carbonate ions → harder to build/maintain CaCO3 skeleton; keep the chain visible rather than stating 'acid dissolves coral'.
Close with argument/evaluation (NGSS MS-LS2-4): which interventions address which cause, and why local fixes (shade, restoration) cannot solve a global chemistry problem.
Use real bleaching-event imagery/data (e.g. Great Barrier Reef events) so the phenomenon is grounded in evidence, not abstraction.
keyRepresentations: Coral polyp cutaway showing zooxanthellae living inside the tissue — the mutualism made visible.
Healthy → bleached → dead colour sequence, paired with a coral energy/food meter to show starvation.
The acidification chain as a labelled flow: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 (carbonic acid) → ↓pH → ↓carbonate ions → weak/dissolving skeleton.
A pH scale/readout falling as CO2 rises, with the ~0.1-unit shift (~30% more acidic) marked.
A reef-dependence panel: the reef structure as habitat for ~25% of marine species, thinning as structure is lost.
commonMisconceptions: 'Bleached coral is dead coral' — bleaching is a stress response; brief bleaching can recover if the algae return, though prolonged bleaching is fatal.
'Coral is a plant' or 'coral bleaches because it loses its own colour' — coral is an animal; most of its colour and food come from the symbiotic algae it expels.
'Bleaching and acidification are the same thing' — one is thermal (heat expels algae), the other chemical (CO2 lowers pH and carbonate); they have different mechanisms and different fixes.
'Acidification means the ocean is turning into acid' — seawater stays slightly alkaline; it is becoming LESS alkaline / more acidic (lower pH), which is enough to reduce carbonate availability.
'Cooling the water or shading reefs would fix everything' — that can relieve bleaching but does nothing for acidification, which only falls with reduced CO2.

learn.summary: Students aged 12–13 learn to distinguish two separate human-driven threats to coral reefs that share one root cause (rising CO2 from burning fossil fuels): thermal bleaching (heat stress makes coral expel its symbiotic algae, losing colour and most of its food) and chemical acidification (dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, lowers pH, reduces carbonate ions, and weakens/dissolves calcium-carbonate skeletons). The core insight is that these are DIFFERENT mechanisms needing different fixes, with reef loss cascading to the ~25% of marine species that depend on reef structure. Activities build from anchoring the coral–algae mutualism, through a two-lever reef model where learners drive temperature and CO2 and observe distinct failures, to argument/evaluation of which interventions address which cause.

activities.title: Drive the reef: two levers, two different failures
feedback: If a learner merges 'hot' and 'acidic' into one vague 'pollution' effect, point to the two separate controls: show that moving only temperature changes colour/food while moving only CO2 changes pH and skeleton.
If a learner says bleached means dead, replay the quick-recovery run: colour returns when heat eases soon, so brief bleaching can recover while prolonged bleaching is fatal.

If a learner expects cooling to fix everything, point to the toggle result: cooling reversed recoverable bleaching but left the acidification damage, so a local/temperature fix cannot solve a global chemistry problem.
When a learner correctly separates the two chains and names CO2 as the shared root, affirm that identifying one cause behind two different attacks is the key idea.
activities.rationale: Two coupled cause→effect chains become concrete when learners drive the inputs and watch a living reef respond, letting the reversible-then-fatal threshold and the mechanism-specific fixes be experienced rather than told. The linked panels (food/energy meter, pH readout, carbonate tokens, species panel) make each mechanism visible; these are illustrative interaction examples, not required implementations.
sourceClaims: Coral bleaching occurs when heat-stressed corals expel their symbiotic zooxanthellae (algae), losing colour and their main energy source; corals can recover if stress is brief but die if it is prolonged. Reefs support around a quarter of marine species.

Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, lowering pH and reducing carbonate ions available to marine calcifiers such as corals, impairing their ability to build and maintain calcium-carbonate skeletons/shells.
learnerActions: Work with a reef model that has two separate controls: water temperature and atmospheric/dissolved CO2.
Raise the TEMPERATURE and describe what happens: zooxanthellae drain out of the polyps, the coral turns white, and a coral food/energy meter falls.
Hold the heat high and observe the coral die; then, in a fresh run, ease the heat back quickly and watch colour return — state in your own words why duration matters, not just peak temperature.

Separately raise the CO2 and describe the different failure: a pH readout falls, carbonate-ion tokens the coral needs to build its skeleton become scarce, growth stalls, and skeleton edges pit and dissolve.
Watch a linked species panel: reef-dependent fish and invertebrates thin out as the reef structure is lost (~25% of marine species).
Test restoration levers (cut emissions, shade/cool the water, plant heat-tolerant coral) and record which lever repairs which failure.

Toggle 'cool the water' after bleaching and acidification have both appeared: note that bleaching recovers — provided the heat stress was not already prolonged to the point of death — while the acidification damage does not budge, and explain what this reveals.
activities.intendedInsight: Bleaching is a reversible-until-it-isn't stress response driven by heat, while acidification is a chemical attack on the skeleton driven by CO2; they are two distinct threats from the same emissions, and only cutting CO2 addresses both.

activities.title: Inside the polyp: anatomy and the two mechanisms
feedback: If a learner calls coral a plant, redirect to the cutaway: coral is an animal that houses algae which photosynthesise and supply most of its energy.
If a learner writes 'acid dissolves coral', ask them to restore the intermediate steps (carbonic acid, lower pH, fewer carbonate ions) so the causal chain stays visible.

If a learner mislabels which state goes with which threat, clarify that the bleached coral is a stressed LIVE animal whose white skeleton shows through transparent tissue after heat-driven algae loss, whereas the pitted/dissolving skeleton is caused by acidification reducing carbonate.
activities.rationale: A clear cutaway and a labelled chemistry chain teach the anatomy and both mechanisms cleanly. This is a strong anchor and consolidation support; because a fixed diagram shows before/after states rather than learner-driven threshold behaviour, pair it with the driven model for the reversible-then-fatal insight.
sourceClaims: Coral bleaching occurs when heat-stressed corals expel their symbiotic zooxanthellae (algae), losing colour and their main energy source; corals can recover if stress is brief but die if it is prolonged. Reefs support around a quarter of marine species.

Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, lowering pH and reducing carbonate ions available to marine calcifiers such as corals, impairing their ability to build and maintain calcium-carbonate skeletons/shells.
learnerActions: Examine a cutaway of a coral polyp and identify the zooxanthellae living inside its tissue; state in your own words that these algae give the coral its colour AND most of its food.

Compare three states side by side — a healthy coloured polyp, a bleached polyp (still a live animal whose transparent tissue reveals the white skeleton beneath after the algae are expelled), and a coral whose skeleton is pitted/dissolving from acidification — and say which threat produced each.
Follow a labelled chemistry chain and fill in the missing steps: CO2 + H2O → carbonic acid (H2CO3) → lower pH → fewer carbonate ions → harder to build/maintain the CaCO3 skeleton.
Write a one-sentence contrast: how the thermal mechanism differs from the chemical mechanism.
activities.intendedInsight: The coral is an animal in mutualism with photosynthetic algae; losing those algae starves it and reveals the white skeleton through its still-living tissue (bleaching), while a separate chemistry chain (CO2→carbonic acid→↓pH→↓carbonate) physically weakens its skeleton (acidification).

activities.title: Does acid attack something hard? Predict–Observe–Explain
feedback: If a learner predicted the hard shell was safe, use the fizzing to surface and name the 'hard things are safe from acid' intuition.
If a learner concludes the ocean is 'turning into acid', correct conservatively: seawater remains slightly alkaline; it is becoming less alkaline (lower pH), which is enough to reduce carbonate ions.

If a learner treats vinegar and seawater as equivalent, restate the caveat: the ocean is far weaker and slower, stays slightly alkaline, and mainly works by lowering carbonate ions so skeletons are harder to build and maintain. It shares the acid–carbonate chemistry but does not visibly fizz like vinegar.
activities.rationale: A concrete predict–observe–explain with a shell or calcium-carbonate chalk in vinegar exposes the 'hard things are safe' intuition and grounds the acid–carbonate reaction in a visible phenomenon before mapping it to the much milder ocean case.
sourceClaims: Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, lowering pH and reducing carbonate ions available to marine calcifiers such as corals, impairing their ability to build and maintain calcium-carbonate skeletons/shells.

Ocean acidification: the ocean has absorbed roughly a quarter to a third of emitted CO2; surface-ocean pH has fallen about 0.1 unit since the industrial era, equivalent to roughly a 30% increase in acidity (hydrogen-ion concentration).
learnerActions: Before observing, write a prediction with a reason: could a weak acid damage something as hard as a seashell or coral skeleton? Most people expect 'no, it's too hard'.

Observe a clean shell or a piece of natural chalk or limestone (calcium carbonate) placed in vinegar; note the immediate fizzing (carbon dioxide gas being released) as the surface is attacked and slowly dissolves. Note: many blackboard chalks are calcium sulfate and will not fizz, so check the material first.
Explain the link to ocean acidification: CO2 makes seawater more acidic, attacking the same calcium carbonate that corals and shellfish build.

State the important caveat in your own words: vinegar is far stronger than seawater, so the ocean effect is much slower and gentler. The shared chemistry is that acid reacts with carbonate, but in the ocean this mainly lowers the number of carbonate ions, making skeletons harder to build and easier to wear away, rather than visibly fizzing them away. Seawater stays slightly alkaline and becomes LESS alkaline, not an actual acid.
activities.intendedInsight: Hard calcium-carbonate structures are not safe from acids; a mildly more acidic ocean is enough to reduce carbonate availability and attack skeletons over time.

activities.title: Interview a reef scientist: trade-offs and evaluation
feedback: If a learner claims shading or restoration can save reefs alone, ask them to trace acidification's cause: lowering water temperature does not remove the extra dissolved CO2, so it cannot reverse the CO2-driven fall in seawater pH.
If a learner cannot name what links warming and acidification, return to the shared root: fossil-fuel CO2 both traps heat and dissolves into seawater.
Credit arguments that explicitly pair an intervention with the cause it addresses and acknowledge trade-offs and uncertainty.
activities.rationale: Open, values-laden evaluation (NGSS MS-LS2-5, evaluating competing solutions for maintaining biodiversity, building on MS-LS2-4) is best handled through argument and discussion once the mechanisms are understood; a responsive interview format lets learners weigh trade-offs a mechanistic model cannot adjudicate.
sourceClaims: Coral bleaching occurs when heat-stressed corals expel their symbiotic zooxanthellae (algae), losing colour and their main energy source; corals can recover if stress is brief but die if it is prolonged. Reefs support around a quarter of marine species.
learnerActions: Interview (in role-play or with a knowledgeable persona) a marine biologist who has surveyed a bleaching event; ask what they saw and why some reefs recover while others do not.
Pose the evaluation questions: is restoration worth it? Should effort go to cutting emissions or to engineering heat-tolerant coral? What has already been lost?
Argue, using the two-mechanism model, why local fixes such as shade, cooling, or restoration help bleaching but cannot solve acidification.
State which interventions target which cause, and why reducing CO2 is the only lever that addresses both.
activities.intendedInsight: Evaluating responses requires matching each intervention to the mechanism it affects; because acidification only eases with reduced CO2, local-only measures are insufficient on their own.

activities.title: Sort and sequence: consolidate the two chains
feedback: If a learner misorders the chain, have them check that each step is caused by the one before (CO2 before carbonic acid, lower pH before fewer carbonate ions).
If a learner miscategorises a symptom, ask whether temperature or CO2 produced it.
If a learner matches cooling to acidification, point out that cooling does not remove the extra dissolved CO2, so it cannot reverse acidification.
activities.rationale: Sequencing, categorisation, and matching can check and consolidate the two-mechanism distinction and the causal chains after the model and chemistry work. This sorting task confirms classification but does not itself elicit the learner-driven, felt model, so use it after the interactive and diagram activities.
sourceClaims: Ocean acidification: the ocean has absorbed roughly a quarter to a third of emitted CO2; surface-ocean pH has fallen about 0.1 unit since the industrial era, equivalent to roughly a 30% increase in acidity (hydrogen-ion concentration).
learnerActions: Sequence the acidification chain in order: CO2 → carbonic acid → lower pH → fewer carbonate ions → weak/dissolving skeleton.
Categorise a mix of symptoms and causes as either bleaching (thermal) or acidification (chemical).
Match each intervention to the cause it addresses (e.g. shading/cooling → bleaching only; cutting emissions → both).
Estimate how much of emitted CO2 the ocean absorbs (~25–30%) and connect that to why ocean pH has fallen about 0.1 unit since the industrial era.
activities.intendedInsight: The two threats have distinct causal chains and distinct fixes; placing each step and symptom in the right chain confirms the learner can keep them separate while recognising the shared CO2 root.

activities.title: Fly through a changing reef (optional immersive view)
feedback: If a learner treats the fly-through as explaining WHY the reef changed, redirect them to the two-lever model and chemistry chain for the mechanism; the fly-through shows the scale of the outcome.
If a learner attributes all the damage to a single cause, ask them to separate the whitening (heat/algae loss) from the structural erosion (CO2/carbonate loss).
activities.rationale: A 3D swim-through can convey scale and the visceral sense of loss that a diagram or dial cannot. Because the concept is chemical/physiological rather than spatial, treat this as an optional engagement/context layer used alongside — not instead of — the driven two-lever model, which may carry the mechanism more efficiently.
learnerActions: Take an optional 3D fly-through over a reef transect and scrub time forward under a combined warming-and-acidifying scenario, watching the reef whiten and erode.
Describe the scale and extent of loss across the transect in your own words.

Connect what you see back to the two mechanisms learned elsewhere: the whitening is heat-driven expulsion of algae, while the crumbling/eroding structure reflects CO2-driven weakening of the skeleton.
activities.intendedInsight: An immersive fly-through may convey the scale and felt sense of reef loss; because the concept is chemical/physiological rather than spatial, this view is less suited to conveying the underlying mechanisms, which are better reached through the two-lever model and chemistry chain. Treat it as a context/engagement layer rather than the primary teacher of mechanism.

constraints: Teach bleaching and acidification as SEPARATE mechanisms with a shared root cause (emissions); do not let learners merge 'hot' and 'acidic' into one vague 'pollution' story.
Anchor bleaching in the mutualism first: learners must know the coral animal depends on the algae for colour AND food before 'expelling the algae' means anything.
Make the reversible-vs-fatal threshold explicit: brief heat stress can recover, prolonged stress kills, so duration and frequency of marine heatwaves matter, not just peak temperature.
Keep the acidification chain visible (CO2 → carbonic acid → ↓pH → fewer carbonate ions → weakened CaCO3 skeleton) rather than collapsing it to 'acid dissolves coral'.

Present bleaching as a stressed LIVE coral whose white skeleton shows through transparent tissue after algae loss — distinct from acidification physically pitting/dissolving the skeleton; do not conflate 'bleached' with an exposed or dead skeleton.
State accurately that seawater stays slightly alkaline and is becoming less alkaline (lower pH); do not say the ocean is 'turning into acid'.
In the vinegar demonstration, make clear vinegar is far stronger than seawater: the demo shows the mechanism, not the ocean's rate or magnitude.

The fixed diagram shows before/after states, not learner-driven threshold behaviour; the sort/sequence task confirms classification rather than eliciting the driven model; the 3D fly-through is better suited to conveying scale than mechanism. Use them alongside, not instead of, activities where learners drive and observe change.
Treat the two-lever model's linked panels, readouts, and tokens as illustrative examples of the learning mechanism, not mandatory features or product requirements.

Local measures (shade, cooling, restoration, heat-tolerant coral) can relieve recoverable bleaching but do not address acidification, which only eases with reduced CO2; present this as the evaluation payoff.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The NOAA coral-bleaching source (claim on zooxanthellae expulsion, recovery vs death, and reefs supporting ~a quarter of marine species) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat the ~25% figure and recovery claims as from an unverified source pending review.

The ~25–30% CO2 absorption and ~0.1 pH-unit / ~30% acidity-increase figures come from a source marked verified:true, but exact figures should be confirmed against current NOAA wording before publication.

The original artefact notes asserted a 3D swim-through 'adds atmosphere, not understanding' and that a static image 'can only show before/after'; these comparative-efficacy/necessity claims are not established by the source evidence and have been softened throughout to scoped affordances with may/less-suited wording. The 3D alternative is retained as an optional activity to preserve the distinct alternative.

No arithmetic or force/motion content required correction; the chemistry chain, the slightly-alkaline framing, and the reversible-only-if-brief bleaching logic were checked and the cooling-toggle action was qualified so no dead/prolonged-bleached coral is implied to revive.

assess.poeTask: Ask the student to PREDICT, with a reason stated first, whether a weak acid could damage something as hard as a seashell or a piece of coral skeleton — most expect 'no, it's too hard'. Drop a clean shell/chalk (calcium carbonate) into vinegar and OBSERVE the immediate fizzing as it is attacked and slowly dissolves. Then EXPLAIN the link to ocean acidification — CO2 makes seawater more acidic, which attacks the same calcium carbonate corals and shellfish build — while noting vinegar is far stronger than seawater, so the ocean effect is slower but works the same way. The pre-observation reason exposes the 'hard things are safe from acid' intuition.
probeDeeper: If a bleached coral can sometimes recover, what does that tell you about whether 'bleached' means 'dead'?
Warming causes bleaching; acidification dissolves skeletons. What single human activity is behind BOTH — and how does one cause produce two different attacks?
Why does losing microscopic algae threaten to starve an animal that can also catch plankton with its tentacles?
Cutting local pollution helps a reef a bit, but scientists say it won't save reefs alone. Given the root cause, why not?
assess.correctAnswer: Bleaching isn't a chemical whitening and the coral isn't necessarily dead. Reef-building corals live in mutualistic symbiosis with tiny photosynthetic algae (zooxanthellae) inside them, which give the coral both colour and most of its food. When water gets too warm, the stressed coral EXPELS the zooxanthellae; without them it loses its colour (you see the white skeleton through clear tissue) and starves — it can recover if conditions ease soon, or die if not. Acidification is a different mechanism: extra CO2 dissolves in seawater to form carbonic acid, lowering the pH and making it harder for corals to build (and easier to dissolve) their calcium carbonate skeletons. But the two threats share ONE root cause — rising CO2 from burning fossil fuels drives BOTH the warming that causes bleaching and the acidification that attacks skeletons.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Bleaching means the coral was chemically whitened / is definitely dead' — reads 'bleach' literally.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe: the white is the coral's own skeleton showing through once it expels its coloured algae under heat stress; it's stressed/starving, and may recover if the heat passes.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the heat bleaches the coral white like bleach on fabric, and a white reef is a dead reef.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says heat 'whitens' the coral like household bleach, or that a bleached reef is always dead; no mention of algae being expelled.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Warming and acidification are unrelated problems' — misses the shared CO2 root.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace both back to fossil-fuel CO2: it traps heat (→ warming → bleaching) AND dissolves into seawater (→ carbonic acid → acidification). One cause, two attacks.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're separate coincidental problems that happen to be harming reefs at the same time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the two as coincidental; can't name what links them; surprised both stem from CO2 emissions.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The coral just makes its own food / the algae are unimportant guests' — misunderstands the mutualism.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Establish mutualism: the zooxanthellae photosynthesise and supply most of the coral's energy; lose them and the coral starves even if unharmed directly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Doesn't see why losing the algae matters; thinks the coral animal feeds itself entirely by catching prey.

responseLevels.gap: Treats bleaching as literal whitening/death and warming and acidification as unrelated; no role for zooxanthellae.
responseLevels.full: Explains bleaching as heat-driven expulsion of symbiotic zooxanthellae (recoverable or fatal), explains acidification as CO2→carbonic acid lowering pH and attacking CaCO3 skeletons, unifies both under rising fossil-fuel CO2, and reasons about why local-only measures are insufficient.
responseLevels.partial: Can describe bleaching as algae loss AND describe acidification chemistry, but as two separate facts — doesn't connect them to a shared CO2 root or link reef loss to wider biodiversity.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A bleached reef is bone-white; nearby, other corals are struggling to build their skeletons at all. A student says 'the heat literally bleached the coral white like bleach does to a T-shirt, and the acid problem is a totally separate thing that just happens to be going on too'. Is a bleached coral 'dead and bleached white', and are warming and acidification two unrelated problems? Explain what actually turns the coral white and what the two threats have in common.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A student with the naive view treats 'bleaching' as literal whitening/death and sees warming and acidification as coincidental; a student with the concept explains bleaching as loss of symbiotic zooxanthellae under heat stress AND identifies CO2 as the common root of both threats. Asking 'what do the two have in common' is the key discriminator — the naive model has no shared cause.
